items.stem: An exam option must be assigned to either 'the kernel' or 'the operating system': providing the full set of interfaces — system calls, plus the libraries and services built on top of them — that lets an application avoid addressing hardware directly. Which is the more precise assignment?

options.text: The operating system, because it is the kernel plus the userspace services and libraries built on it, and that whole layer is what supplies the complete set of interfaces.
options.why: The kernel supplies only the lowest interface, the system call; the rest of that interface set is userspace, so the broader term is the accurate one.

options.text: The kernel, because it is the component that actually schedules the CPU and enforces permissions, so it must also be the source of every interface an application calls.
options.why: The kernel performs the privileged work behind a system call, but libraries and services built above it — part of the OS, not the kernel — supply most of what an application actually calls.

options.text: The distribution, because its package manager installed the libraries the application links against, and whichever component installs a piece of software becomes the layer that interface belongs to.
options.why: Installing a library is a packaging concern; it does not make the distribution the layer that mediates hardware access at runtime.

options.text: Neither term applies cleanly, since applications on Linux address hardware directly once a device file has been opened, with the device file itself standing in for any further mediating software layer.
options.why: Opening a device file still goes through kernel-mediated system calls; a program never gains direct hardware access merely by holding an open file descriptor.

items.rationale: The operating system is the full software layer — kernel plus userspace services and libraries — that intercepts every request an application makes so it need not address hardware directly. The kernel is that layer's most privileged component, not a synonym for the whole of it; treating the two as interchangeable is the exact trap this pairing is built to test.

items.stem: A text editor writes a saved file to disk without containing any code specific to the make or model of the installed disk controller. What makes that possible?

options.text: The operating system mediates the request: the editor calls a general save interface, and the layer beneath translates that into the specific low-level operations the installed controller requires.
options.why: Hiding controller-specific detail behind a general interface is exactly the indirection the operating system exists to provide.

options.text: The everything-is-a-file principle, which lets the editor open the controller's device path directly instead of going through any intermediary layer, since a file path is already a direct handle.
options.why: Everything-is-a-file explains how devices are reached through the filesystem namespace; it does not remove the mediating layer the request still passes through.

options.text: A driver written specifically for that exact controller model was compiled into every Linux kernel in advance, so the editor links against that driver's interface directly rather than a general one.
options.why: Drivers are controller-specific, but the editor never talks to one directly; it calls a general interface that the OS routes onward.

options.text: Modern disk controllers expose a single standardised interface, so no operating-system abstraction is actually needed to write to one, since the hardware itself already presents a uniform API.
options.why: Controllers still vary enough that a driver is required underneath; the standardisation happens at the OS's interface layer, not by eliminating the need for one.

items.rationale: Applications never touch hardware directly. They call OS-provided interfaces, and the OS — kernel plus the services above it — translates that call into whatever the specific installed hardware needs. That indirection is the entire point of the layer.

items.stem: Which single component is directly responsible for scheduling processes onto the CPU, managing memory, and enforcing the permission boundary between them?

options.text: The kernel — the privileged core that performs scheduling, memory management, and permission enforcement itself, with everything else built above it.
options.why: These are the specific responsibilities the guide assigns to the kernel by name, not to the OS as a whole.

options.text: The operating system in general, since 'kernel' is simply informal shorthand people use for the same broader system, the way 'Windows' and 'PC' get used interchangeably.
options.why: The operating system is the broader layer the kernel belongs to; the kernel is its privileged core, not an interchangeable label for it.

options.text: The distribution's init system, since it is the first process started and therefore owns the machine's resources from that point on, ahead of anything the kernel itself does.
options.why: An init system is an ordinary userspace process the kernel starts and schedules like any other; it does not itself perform scheduling or memory management.

options.text: Whichever shell the administrator is currently using, since shell commands are what visibly control processes on the machine and appear to issue every instruction directly.
options.why: A shell only requests process control through system calls; the kernel is what actually performs the scheduling and enforcement behind that request.

items.rationale: The kernel schedules the CPU across processes, manages memory, drives devices, and enforces the permission model. Every other concept in this competency ultimately routes through it, which is why 'what actually does X' questions resolve to the kernel even when the wording says 'Linux' or 'the OS.'

items.stem: An administrator needs the exact release string of the running kernel — the number that would let them check whether a specific driver bug fixed upstream is present on this machine. Which command reports it?

options.text: `uname -r`, which prints the kernel release specifically.
options.why: The `-r` option is documented to report the kernel release, which is precisely the version string a driver-fix check needs.

options.text: `uname -a`, which prints every available field including the kernel release among several others.
options.why: It contains the release string but buries it among hostname, architecture, and build-date fields the task did not ask for; `-r` isolates the one field needed.

options.text: `cat /etc/os-release`, which reports the running system's version.
options.why: That file reports distribution identity, not kernel version; assuming it reports the kernel is the exact mistake the guide's own trap describes.

options.text: `lsmod`, which lists what is currently loaded into the running kernel.
options.why: `lsmod` shows loaded modules, not a version string, and would not answer a question about which kernel release is running.

items.rationale: `uname -r` prints only the kernel's own release string. `uname -a` also includes it but mixed with unrelated fields, and `cat /etc/os-release` answers a different question entirely — distribution identity, not kernel version.

items.stem: A process is run with `sudo` and therefore executes as root. Does that process now run in kernel space?

options.text: No — root is a user-space account privilege; the process still runs in the CPU's restricted execution mode and must still cross a system call to reach the kernel.
options.why: Kernel space is a CPU-enforced execution mode entirely separate from any Unix user account, including root.

options.text: Yes — root has no permission checks applied to it, and having no permission checks is exactly what kernel space means, since nothing is left to restrict what it can touch.
options.why: Fewer permission checks are not the same as a different CPU privilege ring; kernel space names that ring, which root does not enter merely by holding elevated rights.

options.text: Yes, but only while the process is actively performing a privileged system call on the kernel's behalf, since that is when its instructions actually run with elevated rights.
options.why: A system call is the controlled crossing point into kernel space performed by the kernel on the process's behalf; the calling process itself never migrates into that execution mode.

options.text: It depends on the distribution, since some distributions grant root direct kernel-mode execution by default configuration, unlike the more restrictive ones that do not.
options.why: This is a CPU-level distinction with no distribution-specific variation; no mainstream Linux distribution grants a user-space process direct kernel-mode execution.

items.rationale: Kernel space and user space name a CPU-enforced privilege boundary, not a Unix permission level. A root process still runs in user space; it simply has fewer permission checks applied to it there. Only a system call crosses into kernel space, and even then it is the kernel executing, not the calling process itself.

items.stem: A process attempts to read another process's memory directly, without going through any kernel-provided interface. What stops it, and at what level?

options.text: The CPU itself: ordinary processes run in a restricted privilege ring that cannot address arbitrary memory, so the attempt fails at the hardware level before any software policy is even consulted.
options.why: The guide is explicit that the CPU enforces this transition, not just software convention; the ring restriction is a hardware fact, not a permission check.

options.text: The kernel's file permission checks, which reject the read once the attempted access is evaluated against them, the same way any ordinary file read would be checked.
options.why: File permissions govern access to filesystem paths; reading another process's memory directly is not a file operation and is blocked before any such check applies.

options.text: The kernel process itself, which notices the read and terminates the offending process the way a device driver would when it detects unauthorised hardware access.
options.why: This is not a driver-level enforcement mechanism; it is the CPU's privilege-ring architecture that makes the memory unreachable in the first place.

options.text: Nothing at the hardware level — this is purely a software convention that a sufficiently privileged process can simply bypass by asking the kernel nicely enough.
options.why: The guide is explicit that CPU privilege rings enforce this, not software convention alone; that is what makes the boundary meaningful rather than advisory.

items.rationale: The CPU provides hardware privilege levels; ordinary processes run in a restricted one and cannot execute privileged instructions or touch arbitrary memory directly. A process must ask the kernel through a system call, and the CPU — not a software policy alone — enforces that boundary.

items.stem: What distinguishes a system call from an ordinary library function call?

options.text: A system call is the controlled entry point that crosses from user space into the kernel to request privileged work; a library call does not cross that boundary.
options.why: This is the recognition-level distinction the concept exists to test: crossing into the kernel versus staying entirely in userspace.

options.text: A system call always runs faster, because it bypasses the shell's own command-interpretation overhead entirely and talks straight to the running program.
options.why: Speed is not the distinguishing property, and system calls are not defined by any relationship to the shell.

options.text: A system call is written in a different programming language than an ordinary library function is, which is why the two behave so differently at runtime.
options.why: Language choice is an implementation detail; the boundary crossed is what defines a system call, not the language it happens to be written in.

options.text: There is no real distinction; both terms simply describe the same underlying mechanism under different names chosen for historical, not technical, reasons.
options.why: They are not interchangeable: only a system call crosses into the kernel-privileged context, which is exactly the property the term names.

items.rationale: A system call is the controlled entry point by which a userspace program asks the kernel to do privileged work, such as opening a file. A library call that stays in userspace never crosses that boundary at all.

items.stem: A user wants to confirm, from inside their current session, which program is configured as their login shell. Which command reports it?

options.text: `echo $SHELL`, which prints the shell variable holding the user's configured login shell.
options.why: This is exactly the variable the guide names for this purpose, printed with `echo`.

options.text: `echo $PATH`, which lists the shell's search directories including the one holding the shell binary.
options.why: PATH lists directories to search for commands; it does not itself name which program is the user's configured shell.

options.text: `lsblk`, which lists the block devices the shell's history file is stored on.
options.why: Block devices are unrelated to which interpreter is configured as a login shell.

options.text: `$SHELL` always reports the shell that is actually running right now, so the two questions are the same.
options.why: The guide's own trap: `$SHELL` reports the configured login shell, which can differ from the shell currently running if it was overridden after login.

items.rationale: `echo $SHELL` prints the configured login shell. It is worth knowing this can diverge from the shell actually executing a given command, since `$SHELL` is not updated when a different shell is launched interactively.

items.stem: Running `which cd` reports nothing found, yet typing `cd /tmp` at the same prompt works without error. What explains the mismatch?

options.text: `cd` is a shell builtin with no standalone binary on PATH, so the external `which` — which only searches PATH — finds nothing, even though the shell itself executes it directly.
options.why: The guide names `cd` specifically as a builtin that `which` cannot see, which is exactly this symptom.

options.text: The terminal is caching the previous command's output and never actually ran `which cd` at all, which is why nothing new appeared on screen.
options.why: The terminal only renders input and output; it does not cache or intercept command execution, so this does not explain the result.

options.text: PATH is misconfigured and missing the directory that would normally contain the `cd` executable, since every runnable command needs a directory entry somewhere on that list.
options.why: No directory ever contains a `cd` binary on a standard system, because `cd` is a builtin rather than an installed executable; PATH is not the issue.

options.text: `which` is broken on this system, since it should be able to find every command that actually runs successfully, builtin or not.
options.why: `which` is working as designed; it deliberately only searches PATH for external executables and has no visibility into shell builtins by design.

items.rationale: Some commands, `cd` among them, are shell builtins with no standalone binary on a Linux system. The external `which` only searches PATH, so it correctly reports nothing found for a builtin even though the shell itself runs it directly.

items.stem: A user reports 'my terminal is frozen.' A foreground command is actually hung waiting on network I/O, and the terminal emulator itself is rendering fine. Was the report accurate?

options.text: No — the terminal is displaying correctly; it is the shell's foreground command that is hung, which needs a signal (Ctrl-C) rather than restarting the terminal emulator.
options.why: Casual speech conflates the two, but the fix differs: a genuinely frozen emulator needs killing at the window-manager level, a hung command needs a signal instead.

options.text: Yes — 'terminal' and 'shell' name the same thing, so a hung shell command is by definition the terminal itself freezing, with no meaningful difference between the two at all.
options.why: The terminal displays; the shell interprets and forks commands. They are routinely conflated in speech, but they are different programs with different fixes.

options.text: No — the report describes a kernel scheduling failure, since only the kernel can cause a process to stop responding at all, regardless of what it is waiting on.
options.why: Waiting on network I/O is ordinary blocking behaviour, not a kernel scheduling failure; nothing here implicates the kernel itself.

options.text: Yes — any unresponsive prompt is, by definition, a frozen terminal no matter what is actually blocking it, since the symptom looks identical either way.
options.why: Treating every unresponsive prompt as a terminal problem is exactly the looseness the exam exploits; the description here points at the shell's foreground command, not the display program.

items.rationale: The terminal manages display and input; the shell interprets commands. A command hung on I/O is a shell-side condition needing a signal to the process, not a terminal-emulator restart — even though users describe both situations as 'the terminal froze.'

items.stem: An SSH session into a remote server presents a working command prompt. What role is the SSH session filling in this picture?

options.text: It is acting as the terminal — it carries keyboard input to the remote shell and renders the shell's output back, without interpreting any of the commands itself.
options.why: A remote session over SSH is named directly as a modern form of terminal in the guide, alongside a physical device or a terminal emulator window.

options.text: It is acting as the shell, since it is what the user directly interacts with to type and run commands, exactly the role a local shell prompt would otherwise play.
options.why: Direct interaction does not make it the interpreter; the remote shell running on the server does the interpreting, the SSH session only carries the input and output.

options.text: It is acting as the kernel, since it manages the network connection that carries the session's data all the way from the client to the server.
options.why: Network connection handling is a kernel-level detail on both ends, but that does not make the SSH session itself a kernel component.

options.text: It is acting as a pseudo-terminal device, which is a kernel object rather than anything the SSH client itself supplies over the connection.
options.why: A pty is the kernel-side channel the terminal and shell communicate over; the SSH session itself is the terminal program using that channel, not the channel itself.

items.rationale: The terminal, historically a physical device, is today usually a terminal emulator window or a remote session over SSH. It manages display and input and hands typed input to whatever program it launched — usually a shell — over a pseudo-terminal device.

items.stem: An administrator wants live CPU information and runs `cat /proc/cpuinfo` rather than a dedicated tool. What Unix design principle makes that command meaningful?

options.text: Everything is a file: devices, sockets, and kernel state are exposed through the same filesystem interface used for ordinary files, so `cat` can read them like any other path.
options.why: The principle is exactly that pseudo-filesystems like `/proc` expose live kernel state as readable text through the same open/read calls as a regular file.

options.text: Multi-user isolation, since `/proc/cpuinfo` is scoped separately per logged-in user session, the way a user's own files and settings normally are.
options.why: `/proc/cpuinfo` reports machine-wide hardware facts and is not a per-user isolated resource; multi-user isolation is a different design property.

options.text: The kernel-space/user-space boundary, since crossing it is what makes `cat` able to read kernel data at all, regardless of where that particular data happens to physically live on disk.
options.why: That boundary explains why a system call is needed at all; it does not explain why the data is reachable at a filesystem path in the first place, which is the file-abstraction principle.

options.text: `/proc/cpuinfo` is a regular text file the kernel writes to disk at boot and never touches again, the same as any other static configuration file.
options.why: It is a pseudo-file backed by live kernel state, generated on read rather than stored on disk, which is why it always reflects current information.

items.rationale: The kernel presents devices and interfaces as special file types, alongside pseudo-filesystems like `/proc` and `/sys`, using the same open/read/write/close calls as ordinary files. That is why so many 'how do I check X' answers reduce to reading a path.

items.stem: Which pair of paths best illustrates that devices and ordinary data are reached through the same interface on Linux?

options.text: `/dev/sda` for a disk device and `/home/user/notes.txt` for a document, both opened, read, and written with the same system calls.
options.why: A device file and a regular file both go through open/read/write/close identically, which is the whole point of the principle.

options.text: `/etc/passwd` and `/etc/shadow`, since both concern user account information specifically and sit in the same configuration directory.
options.why: Both are ordinary configuration files; the pairing says nothing about devices being reached through the file interface, which is what the principle is about.

options.text: `/proc/cpuinfo` and `lscpu`'s output, since both ultimately describe the same CPU information in slightly different formats.
options.why: One is a path and the other is a command's formatted output; comparing them does not illustrate the file-interface principle, only that a tool can read that path.

options.text: Any two paths under `/etc`, since configuration files are the clearest example 'everything is a file' offers to a new user.
options.why: Ordinary configuration files were always files; the principle is specifically about non-file things — devices, sockets, kernel state — being exposed the same way, not about configuration.

items.rationale: The principle's force is in unifying access to things that are not intuitively files — a disk device, a socket, live kernel state — with ordinary files, all reached through open/read/write/close. Pairing a device path with a document file shows that unification directly.

items.stem: Two different users are logged into the same server at once, each running a process with the identical program name. Why does this not cause a conflict?

options.text: The kernel schedules and owns each process separately, keeping their memory and permissions apart regardless of which program name either one happens to share.
options.why: Multi-user, multitasking isolation is what the guide names as the reason two same-named processes coexist without interfering.

options.text: The shell renames one of the two processes automatically to avoid any naming collision between them at the operating-system level.
options.why: Shells do not rename running processes to avoid collisions; process identity is tracked by process ID, not by program name uniqueness.

options.text: Each user is confined to a separate kernel running in its own lightweight container on the host, fully isolated from every other logged-in user's kernel instance.
options.why: Standard multi-user Linux runs one kernel shared by all logged-in users; per-user kernel isolation is not what makes this scenario safe.

options.text: Only one of the two processes can actually be running at a time; the OS silently queues the second behind it until the first one exits.
options.why: Both processes genuinely run concurrently, time-sliced across the CPU; neither is silently queued behind the other.

items.rationale: Linux is designed to run many users and many processes concurrently, each isolated from the others by the kernel. Process ownership and permission checks are what let identically named processes coexist safely, whoever launched them.

items.stem: A user sends a termination signal intending to stop their own runaway process, but a colleague's identically-named process is also running on the shared server. What design guarantees the signal reaches only the intended process?

options.text: The multi-user, multitasking design: process ownership and permission checks mean a signal from one user cannot reach another user's process by default, regardless of shared program names.
options.why: This is the coherent system of permission checks the guide says exists precisely because Linux assumes many users and processes running concurrently.

options.text: The shell resolves the signal target by matching PATH first, so it always finds the sender's own binary to signal instead of anyone else's.
options.why: PATH resolves command names to executables when launching a program; it plays no role in routing a signal to an already-running process.

options.text: Signals are addressed to a program name rather than a process ID, so ownership never enters into it at any point in the delivery process.
options.why: Signals target a specific process ID, and the kernel's ownership check on that ID — not the program's name — is what prevents cross-user interference.

options.text: Nothing guarantees this; two identically named processes running under different users on the same shared server are a known race condition that occasionally kills the wrong one without warning.
options.why: This is exactly the assumption the multi-user design is built to prevent: ownership and permission checks, not naming, determine which process a signal can reach.

items.rationale: Every permission model in this domain rests on the assumption that many users and processes run concurrently, isolated by the kernel. Process ownership — not the program's name — is what a signal's permission check is actually evaluated against.

items.stem: A script needs to identify which distribution it is running on before choosing between `apt` and `dnf`. Which command reads the machine-readable identity file for that purpose?

options.text: `cat /etc/os-release`, which prints the standard distribution identity file every installed system carries.
options.why: This is the specific standard, machine-readable file the guide names for identifying a distribution.

options.text: `uname -r`, which reports the running kernel version so the script can infer the distribution from that number.
options.why: `uname -r` reports only the kernel release; the kernel version does not by itself identify which distribution is installed.

options.text: `uname -a`, which prints a full summary that includes the operating system name field., a related but functionally different command whose behaviour does not match what the scenario is actually asking for
options.why: It can include an OS name field on some builds, but it does not report the distribution's specific identity the way `/etc/os-release` does.

options.text: `lsblk`, which lists the disks the distribution's files happen to be installed on.
options.why: Block device listings say nothing about which distribution is installed; they describe storage, not software identity.

items.rationale: `/etc/os-release` is the standard, machine-readable file carrying a distribution's identity. `uname -r` answers a different question — kernel version — which the guide's own trap warns against confusing with distribution identity.

items.stem: 'Which distribution is this' and 'which distribution family is this' are asked about the same server. Do they expect the same answer?

options.text: No — the distribution names one specific installable system (for example Ubuntu 24.04), while the family names the packaging lineage it shares with others (the Debian family).
options.why: Granularity is the separating axis: a distribution is a singular product, a family is a category spanning several products.

options.text: Yes — a kernel version determines both the distribution and its family identically, since the exact same kernel build is assumed to ship inside every distribution that uses it at all.
options.why: Kernel version identifies neither a distribution nor its family on its own; the kernel is one component shared across an entire family.

options.text: No, but only because Arch has no family at all, unlike every other Linux distribution currently in wide use today.
options.why: Arch does belong to a family — its own, built around `pacman` and a rolling model — so this is not the reason the two questions diverge.

options.text: No real distinction exists; 'distribution' and 'family' are used interchangeably even in careful technical writing about Linux systems.
options.why: The exam tests this precisely because they are not interchangeable — RHEL and Fedora are different distributions in the same family, which only makes sense if the terms differ.

items.rationale: A distribution is one specific product a person installs. A family is the packaging lineage several distributions share. RHEL and Fedora being 'different distributions in the same family' only makes sense once that distinction is held separately.

items.stem: Given `ID=fedora` in a system's `/etc/os-release`, which package manager and package format should be expected?

options.text: `dnf`, using `.rpm` packages — Fedora belongs to the Red Hat family.
options.why: Fedora is a Red Hat-family distribution, and `dnf`/`.rpm` is that family's tooling.

options.text: `apt`, using `.deb` packages, since Fedora is commonly assumed to follow the same lineage as Ubuntu.
options.why: That assumption pairs Fedora with the Debian family; Fedora is Red Hat-family and uses `dnf`, not `apt` — a pure recall failure the exam is built to catch.

options.text: `zypper`, using `.rpm` packages, since Fedora and openSUSE are both `.rpm`-based.
options.why: Sharing a package format does not mean sharing a family's tooling; `zypper` belongs to SUSE, not Red Hat, even though both use `.rpm`.

options.text: Whichever manager the administrator prefers, since package format is a matter of local configuration rather than distribution identity.
options.why: Package format and manager are fixed by the distribution's family, not by local preference; installing a foreign package manager does not change what the distribution ships with by default.

items.rationale: Fedora is in the Red Hat family, which uses `.rpm` packages and `dnf`. Package-manager questions are literal recall: given a distribution name, its family's tooling follows directly.

items.stem: A colleague claims 'CentOS Stream is just CentOS Linux under a new name, still safe to treat as a fixed, stable release.' What is wrong with that claim?

options.text: CentOS Stream is a rolling preview of upcoming RHEL, not a continuation of the discontinued, fixed-release CentOS Linux; Rocky Linux is the actual fixed-release replacement.
options.why: The guide names this exact confusion as a trap: Stream previews what RHEL will become, it does not stand in for the old fixed-release product.

options.text: Nothing is wrong — both are Red Hat family distributions sharing the same `dnf` package manager and `.rpm` format, so the naming difference carries no practical operational weight at all.
options.why: Sharing a family's tooling does not make two products interchangeable; release stability and support model differ sharply between a rolling preview and a fixed release.

options.text: The claim is wrong only about the package manager, since CentOS Stream switched to `apt` at some point during its development.
options.why: CentOS Stream remains `.rpm`/`dnf`-based, staying within the Red Hat family; the package manager was never the issue with the claim.

options.text: The claim is essentially correct; 'Stream' only refers to a faster update channel within that same fixed-release product line.
options.why: This restates the misconception rather than correcting it — Stream previews upcoming RHEL and is not the discontinued fixed-release CentOS Linux at all.

items.rationale: CentOS Stream is not CentOS Linux — it is a rolling preview of upcoming RHEL, not the discontinued fixed-release CentOS Linux. Rocky Linux exists specifically as CentOS Linux's downstream, fixed-release replacement.

items.stem: A production database server must not have package behaviour shift unexpectedly underneath a running service. Which release policy fits that requirement, and why?

options.text: An LTS release, because its package versions stay frozen after release and only security-relevant patches are backported into those same versions.
options.why: Stability against currency is the exact trade-off: LTS changes least over its support life, which is what a production server needs most.

options.text: A rolling release, because it always runs the newest software and therefore carries the fewest known bugs at any given time.
options.why: Newest is not safest for a running service — rolling releases update continuously, which is exactly the shifting behaviour the requirement rules out.

options.text: Whichever release the distribution family recommends, since family and release policy amount to one single decision.
options.why: Release policy is a separate axis from family; Ubuntu, in the Debian family, still offers both an LTS and a non-LTS track.

options.text: Rolling releases also freeze versions, they just do it more frequently, so either policy satisfies the requirement equally well over a long enough window.
options.why: A rolling release has no freeze at all — updates flow continuously with no single version to point to — which is the opposite of what the requirement asks for.

items.rationale: LTS releases freeze a version and backport only security and bug fixes for a fixed window; rolling releases ship every update continuously with no freeze at all. For a production system where shifting behaviour is the bigger risk, LTS is the safer choice.

items.stem: What is the practical cost a team accepts by choosing a rolling release over an LTS release?

options.text: More frequent, active maintenance — updates arrive continuously, and the team must absorb behaviour changes as they land rather than on a scheduled cadence.
options.why: The trade-off is explicit: rolling systems run the newest software at the cost of needing more frequent, active maintenance.

options.text: A shorter support window before the distribution stops receiving any updates whatsoever, forcing a much earlier reinstall than an LTS user would ever expect.
options.why: Support windows and end-of-life dates are an LTS-track concept; a rolling release has no comparable fixed support window to fall short of.

options.text: A different package manager than the one the distribution family would normally use for its releases.
options.why: Release policy does not change which package manager a distribution uses; Arch's `pacman` is tied to the distribution, not to being a rolling release.

options.text: None — rolling releases are strictly an improvement on LTS with no offsetting cost at all worth mentioning.
options.why: The guide frames this explicitly as a trade-off, not a strict improvement: currency is gained at the cost of stability and maintenance burden.

items.rationale: Rolling releases ship continuously with no version to freeze, trading stability for currency. That currency has to be actively managed, which is the real cost against an LTS track that changes only on a scheduled, security-focused basis.

items.stem: A colleague says their laptop 'runs Linux' and separately that it 'runs GNU/Linux.' Are those two statements necessarily equivalent?

options.text: No — 'Linux' names the kernel alone and is always accurate wherever that kernel runs; 'GNU/Linux' names that kernel specifically paired with a GNU userland, which not every Linux system has.
options.why: Android is the guide's own counter-example: it runs the Linux kernel with a non-GNU userland, so 'Linux' is the safer umbrella term.

options.text: Yes — the kernel is the only component that genuinely matters here, so any userland running on top of it counts as GNU regardless of where that userland actually came from or who originally wrote it.
options.why: The kernel is one component; the userland running above it is a separate choice, and Android's Bionic userland shows it need not be GNU at all.

options.text: No, but only because GNU refers to a licensing status rather than an actual body of software anyone can point to.
options.why: GNU names a concrete body of software — the compiler, shell, and core utilities from the GNU Project — not merely a license category.

options.text: Yes, since the Linux Foundation requires every certified Linux distribution to ship a GNU userland as a condition of certification.
options.why: No such requirement exists, and the Linux Foundation does not control userland composition; GNU/Linux describes an actual pairing that some systems, like Android, do not have.

items.rationale: Linux, strictly, is the kernel Linus Torvalds began in 1991. Most Linux userlands trace to the GNU Project, which is why the pairing is sometimes called GNU/Linux — but not every Linux system has a GNU userland, so the two phrases are not interchangeable.

items.stem: What did the GNU Project supply before the Linux kernel existed, and what was it still missing?

options.text: A compiler, a shell, core utilities, and most of the GPL licensing framework — everything except a free kernel of its own, which Linux later filled.
options.why: The guide states this directly: GNU supplied nearly the whole system years before Linux existed, lacking only a free kernel.

options.text: A complete operating system including its own kernel, which Linux later replaced for better overall performance.
options.why: GNU had no kernel of its own at the time; Linux did not replace an existing GNU kernel, it filled the one piece GNU was missing.

options.text: A package manager and release policy, which every GNU/Linux distribution still relies on today for updates.
options.why: Package managers and release policies are distribution-level decisions, not something the GNU Project itself supplied historically.

options.text: Nothing substantial — GNU contributed little more than a name before Linux ever arrived, with essentially no working software behind it at that point.
options.why: GNU supplied the compiler (GCC), the shell, core utilities, and the GPL years before Linux existed, which is why the pairing became so natural once a kernel was available.

items.rationale: GNU, begun in 1983, supplied the compiler, shell, core utilities, and most of the license framework years before Linux existed in 1991. It lacked only a free kernel, which the Linux project filled — hence GNU/Linux for the combination.

items.stem: Who sets the Linux kernel's technical direction, and what role does the Linux Foundation actually play in that?

options.text: Torvalds and the kernel's maintainer hierarchy set technical direction; the Linux Foundation sponsors and hosts development infrastructure and funds core maintainers, an organisational role rather than a technical one.
options.why: The guide draws this distinction directly: governance stays with the maintainer hierarchy, sponsorship and hosting sit with the Foundation.

options.text: The Linux Foundation sets technical direction, since its name appears on the certification program and it directly employs a large number of the kernel's most active and visible contributors working on it today.
options.why: Employing contributors and lending its name to a certification are sponsorship activities; the Foundation does not decide which patches merge or set the kernel's direction.

options.text: Torvalds alone personally decides every single patch that merges, without any maintainer hierarchy standing beneath him at any level of the project.
options.why: Subsystem maintainers review and merge the vast majority of patches, escalating disputed changes upward; Torvalds is the top of a hierarchy, not the sole reviewer.

options.text: A vote among major distribution vendors decides technical direction, coordinated entirely through the Foundation's regular meetings.
options.why: The Foundation provides neutral ground for vendors to collaborate, but kernel technical decisions run through the maintainer hierarchy, not a vendor vote.

items.rationale: Kernel development runs through a maintainer hierarchy escalating to Torvalds. The Linux Foundation provides infrastructure, funding, and trademark stewardship — sponsorship and hosting, not technical governance.

items.stem: In what year, and in what capacity, did Linus Torvalds begin the Linux kernel?

options.text: 1991, as a free Unix-like kernel he then developed openly with a growing contributor base.
options.why: This is the founding fact the guide states plainly, distinct from any later organisational involvement.

options.text: 1991, as an official Linux Foundation project from its founding.
options.why: The Linux Foundation did not exist in 1991; it was founded later and took on a sponsoring role after the kernel was already an established open project.

options.text: 1983, as part of the GNU Project's effort to build a complete free Unix-like system.
options.why: 1983 is when the GNU Project itself began; Linux started later, in 1991, as the missing kernel piece GNU still lacked.

options.text: The exact year is disputed, since the kernel's development predates any reliable public record.
options.why: 1991 is well documented and not in dispute; the kernel's early history is one of the better-recorded parts of its story.

items.rationale: Torvalds began the Linux kernel in 1991 as a free Unix-like kernel, developing it openly with a large contributor base ever since — years before the Linux Foundation existed to sponsor it.

items.stem: A shell script written and tested on Linux mostly works unmodified on another Unix-like system. What property of Linux explains that portability?

options.text: Linux is Unix-like and largely POSIX-conformant, and that conformance is why skills and scripts port across Unix-like systems.
options.why: This is the recognition-level fact the concept tests: POSIX conformance is the reason for the portability, not an incidental detail.

options.text: The GPLv2 license under which the kernel is released is what guarantees behavioural compatibility across every Unix-like system.
options.why: Licensing terms govern redistribution rights, not runtime command or system-call behaviour; they are unrelated to script portability.

options.text: Every Unix-like system runs the same underlying kernel, so scripts naturally behave identically everywhere.
options.why: Different Unix-like systems run entirely different kernels; the shared standard is POSIX conformance, not a shared kernel.

options.text: Shell scripts are portable by nature and would run the same on any operating system regardless of any standard at all.
options.why: Portability across Unix-like systems specifically follows from shared POSIX conformance; it does not extend to unrelated operating systems without that conformance.

items.rationale: Linux is Unix-like and largely POSIX-conformant, which is why skills and scripts port across Unix systems sharing that conformance. It is a recognition-level fact: know that conformance is the reason, not the contents of the standard.

items.stem: Under exactly which license terms is the Linux kernel released?

options.text: GPLv2 only — not 'GPLv2 or later' — which is why the exact clause is worth holding separately from other GPL-licensed software.
options.why: The guide is explicit that this is GPLv2-only, contrasted with the more common 'or later' clause seen elsewhere.

options.text: MIT, chosen specifically to make commercial redistribution far simpler for vendors than the copyleft terms of the GPL would otherwise allow.
options.why: The kernel is not MIT-licensed; MIT is a permissive license and does not carry the GPL's copyleft requirement the kernel actually operates under.

options.text: GPLv2 or later, matching the clause used by most other GNU Project software packages and tools.
options.why: The kernel deliberately uses GPLv2 only, not the 'or later' clause common elsewhere in GNU software — this is the specific fact the concept tests.

options.text: Whatever license the distribution packaging it chooses to apply on top of it during packaging.
options.why: A distribution cannot override the kernel's own license; userland tools bundled alongside it may carry different licenses individually, but the kernel itself stays GPLv2.

items.rationale: The kernel is released under GPLv2 only, not the more common 'GPLv2 or later' clause. This is why distributions may copy, modify, and redistribute it, provided redistributions stay under that same license.

items.stem: A company wants to redistribute a modified version of the Linux kernel as part of a commercial appliance. What does GPLv2 require of them?

options.text: The redistributed derivative must also be licensed under GPLv2, and the corresponding source code must be made available to recipients.
options.why: Copyleft is the operative mechanism: anyone may modify and redistribute, but a derivative must stay under GPLv2 with source made available.

options.text: Nothing — GPLv2 permits silent commercial redistribution with no source obligation attached whatsoever, unlike stricter copyleft licenses.
options.why: GPLv2 is copyleft precisely because it does impose a source-availability obligation on redistribution, unlike a permissive license that would not.

options.text: They must switch the derivative to a permissive license before selling it, since GPLv2 forbids commercial use outright by design.
options.why: GPLv2 explicitly permits commercial redistribution; it does not forbid selling the software, it only requires the derivative to remain under GPLv2 with source available.

options.text: They must contribute the change back to the upstream kernel project before shipping the appliance at all.
options.why: GPLv2 requires making source available to recipients of the redistribution; it does not require contributing changes back to any upstream project.

items.rationale: GPLv2 is copyleft: anyone may run, study, modify, and redistribute the code, but a redistributed derivative must also be licensed under GPLv2 with source made available to recipients. Commercial use is permitted; the obligation is about license and source, not about selling.

items.stem: A batch job needs to know how many processing units are actually available to it right now, which may be fewer than the machine's physical total under a cgroup limit. Which command answers that specifically?

options.text: `nproc`, which reports the number of processing units currently available to the calling process.
options.why: The guide names `nproc` specifically as reporting what is available to the caller, not the unconstrained physical total.

options.text: `lscpu`, whose default summary reports the full installed CPU topology rather than what is available to the caller.
options.why: `lscpu` formats the machine's overall topology; it does not account for a cgroup or affinity restriction on the calling process the way `nproc` does.

options.text: `free -h`, since memory and CPU limits are reported together under cgroups.
options.why: `free -h` reports memory and swap usage; it says nothing about how many processing units a process can use.

options.text: `nproc --all` and plain `nproc` always report the same number, so either serves the purpose.
options.why: `--all` counts all installed processors regardless of restriction, while plain `nproc` reports what is currently available to the caller — exactly the distinction this task needs.

items.rationale: `nproc` reports processing units currently available to the calling process, which can be fewer than the physical total under cgroup or affinity constraints. `lscpu` describes the machine's overall topology instead.

items.stem: `lscpu` reports 'CPU(s): 16' on a machine with 8 physical cores and simultaneous multithreading enabled. Is 16 the physical core count?

options.text: No — with hyperthreading, the logical processor count exceeds the physical core count; `lscpu` separates sockets, cores, and threads explicitly in its fuller output.
options.why: This is the guide's own trap: 'number of CPUs' is ambiguous between sockets, physical cores, and logical processors, and 16 here counts logical processors.

options.text: Yes — `lscpu`'s 'CPU(s)' line always reports physical cores regardless of any SMT or hyperthreading settings enabled.
options.why: That line reports logical processors, which include SMT threads; reading it as physical cores is exactly the misreading the guide warns about.

options.text: The discrepancy means the machine actually has two separate CPU architectures installed side by side on one board.
options.why: Nothing about SMT implies multiple architectures; hyperthreading multiplies the logical count on a single architecture's physical cores.

options.text: `lscpu` is reporting a fault, since the number of CPUs should always equal the physical socket count exactly, with no legitimate exceptions permitted on real hardware.
options.why: This is expected, correct behaviour for a system with SMT enabled; it is not a fault, and 'CPU(s)' was never defined to mean socket count.

items.rationale: 'Number of CPUs' is ambiguous between sockets, physical cores, and logical processors — with hyperthreading, logical count exceeds physical cores. `lscpu`'s fuller output separates these explicitly, avoiding the misreading.

items.stem: `free -h` shows a small 'free' figure and a large 'used' figure on a server that feels fine. Which column should actually be trusted to judge whether the system is memory-constrained?

options.text: 'available' — it estimates what a new process could actually get, correctly accounting for reclaimable cache that the raw 'free' column does not credit back.
options.why: The guide is explicit that 'free' looks misleadingly low because idle RAM is being used as disk cache; 'available' is the honest figure for this judgement.

options.text: 'free', since it is treated as a persistent block device figure and therefore the single most reliable measure of headroom available anywhere on the running system.
options.why: 'free' is a RAM figure, not a storage-device one, and it is exactly the column the guide warns against trusting for pressure judgements.

options.text: 'used', since a large 'used' figure always means the system is close to the OOM killer no matter the surrounding context.
options.why: 'used' in `free`'s output already excludes reclaimable cache and is the honest figure, but a large value alone does not by itself confirm OOM proximity without checking swap.

options.text: None of the columns matter; only `uptime`'s load average actually determines memory pressure on a running system.
options.why: Load average measures CPU contention, not memory state; `free`'s own columns are what is needed to judge memory pressure specifically.

items.rationale: The kernel uses otherwise-idle RAM as disk cache, so the raw 'free' column looks low even when memory is not actually constrained. `free`'s 'available' column is the one that estimates real headroom for a new process.

items.stem: A process's memory usage keeps climbing until it is abruptly terminated with no warning in its own logs. What kernel mechanism most likely explains the termination?

options.text: The out-of-memory (OOM) killer, invoked under severe memory pressure to reclaim RAM by terminating a process.
options.why: Under severe pressure the kernel's OOM killer is exactly the mechanism that terminates a process to reclaim memory, independent of anything the process itself logs.

options.text: Swap exhaustion causing the storage device holding the swap file to fail outright.
options.why: Swap running low slows the system by paging heavily; it does not itself terminate a process the way the OOM killer does.

options.text: The scheduler deprioritising the process until it starves of CPU time entirely.
options.why: Starving for CPU time causes slowness, not termination; only the OOM killer actually ends a process to reclaim memory.

options.text: Processes on Linux are never terminated by the OS itself; this must have been an explicit `kill` from another user.
options.why: The OOM killer is a real, kernel-initiated termination mechanism specifically for reclaiming memory under pressure, distinct from any user-issued signal.

items.rationale: When RAM is exhausted, the kernel either swaps pages to disk, slowing sharply, or under severe pressure invokes the OOM killer to terminate a process and reclaim memory — which explains an abrupt termination with no corresponding application-level warning.

items.stem: `lsblk` output shows `sda` as a parent row with `sda1` and `sda2` indented beneath it. Treating `sda1` as if it were the entire disk, what mistake follows?

options.text: Acting on the wrong device — `sda1` is one partition of the whole disk `sda`, and operations meant for the full disk would then target only part of it.
options.why: The guide names this specific misreading: treating a partition row as if it were the whole disk and acting on the wrong device.

options.text: Assuming the stored data will be permanently lost on the next reboot, since only volatile RAM contents are ever known to reset in that particular way.
options.why: Reboot data loss is a property of volatile RAM, not of a storage partition; `sda1` persists across reboots like any other block device.

options.text: Believing the filesystem type is always ext4 unless `-f` is explicitly passed as a flag to `lsblk`.
options.why: `-f` reveals filesystem type and UUID, which are absent from the default columns, but that omission is a different mistake than confusing a partition with its parent disk.

options.text: No real mistake follows, since `sda` and `sda1` always hold exactly identical data at every point in time.
options.why: A partition and its parent disk are not identical; the parent spans the whole device while a partition is one region of it, so operations differ in scope.

items.rationale: `lsblk` presents whole disks as parents and partitions as children in its hierarchy. Treating a partition row like `sda1` as the whole disk `sda` means acting on the wrong device — a common, testable misreading.

items.stem: A monitoring dashboard shows both 'RAM usage' and 'disk usage' climbing together and a teammate assumes they must be the same underlying resource. What single property actually separates them?

options.text: Volatility and access pattern: RAM is volatile and byte-addressable, cleared on power loss; storage devices are persistent and block-addressable through a filesystem and driver.
options.why: The guide's own comparison names persistence as the separating axis, with byte-addressable RAM on one side and block-addressable storage on the other.

options.text: Nothing meaningfully separates the two — both simply hold data the system needs, so 'usage' means exactly the same thing for either one regardless of context or how it is measured.
options.why: RAM and storage differ sharply in what exhausting them causes — swapping or the OOM killer for RAM, write failures for storage — so treating 'usage' as identical loses that distinction.

options.text: RAM is managed by the kernel while storage devices are managed entirely by user-space drivers instead of the kernel.
options.why: Both RAM allocation and storage device access are kernel-managed; the distinction is not about which layer manages them.

options.text: Storage devices are addressed through system calls while RAM is addressed without any kernel involvement at all in the process.
options.why: RAM access by a process is also mediated by the kernel's memory management; the difference is volatility and addressing granularity, not kernel involvement.

items.rationale: RAM is volatile and byte-addressable, directly by the CPU; storage devices are persistent and block-addressable through a filesystem and driver. Exhausting one causes swapping or an OOM kill; exhausting the other causes write failures — different failure modes following from that one axis.

items.stem: A deployment pipeline needs the machine's instruction set architecture to pick the right container image tag. Which command reports it, using the option that reports machine hardware name specifically?

options.text: `uname -m`, whose `-m` option reports the machine hardware name — `x86_64` or `aarch64` — the CPU instruction set the kernel was built for.
options.why: The guide names `-m` specifically for machine hardware name, distinct from `-r` for kernel release.

options.text: `uname -r`, since it is the same command and any option returns comparable system information., a command from the same family that solves an adjacent problem rather than the one described in the scenario
options.why: `-r` reports kernel release, a version string, not the hardware architecture; confusing the two options answers a different question than the one asked.

options.text: `lscpu`, since architecture information never appears anywhere in its output at all.
options.why: `lscpu` does include architecture in its summary, but the task specifically calls for the machine hardware name via `uname -m`, the concept's own recorded command.

options.text: `arch` and `uname -m` can disagree on the same machine, so both should be checked and reconciled manually.
options.why: On Linux, `arch` is effectively a thin wrapper around the same value `uname -m` reports; assuming disagreement is possible is the guide's stated trap.

items.rationale: `uname -m` reports the machine hardware name via its `-m` option, distinct from `-r`'s kernel release. `arch` reports the same value as a thin wrapper, so the two commands do not disagree on Linux.

items.stem: A container image built for `linux/amd64` fails to start on a host where `uname -m` reports `aarch64`, with an unhelpful generic error. What kind of problem is this most likely to be?

options.text: An architecture mismatch — the image's instruction set does not match the host's, not a missing dependency inside the image.
options.why: This exact symptom is named directly: an architecture mismatch producing an unhelpful failure message, easily misread as a missing-package error.

options.text: A missing kernel module for the container runtime, unrelated to the image's intended target platform entirely.
options.why: Nothing in the scenario points at a missing driver; the architecture strings named — `amd64` versus `aarch64` — are what identify the actual cause.

options.text: A kernel version mismatch, since `uname` is the very command that surfaced the problem in the first place.
options.why: `uname -m` reports hardware architecture specifically; a kernel version mismatch would involve `uname -r`, a different field entirely.

options.text: The error is unrelated to architecture, since containers are architecture-independent by design entirely, according to this claim.
options.why: Container images and binaries are architecture-specific; one built for one instruction set will not run natively on another without emulation, which is exactly this failure.

items.rationale: Binaries and container images are architecture-specific. `amd64` naming a target that does not match the host's `aarch64` is an architecture mismatch, not a missing dependency — recognising the symptom avoids wrong-direction debugging.

items.stem: A new peripheral does not work. `lsmod` shows no module related to it. What is the correct next step before concluding a module needs to be loaded?

options.text: Check whether a suitable module exists to load with `modprobe` — but also consider that the driver might be compiled directly into the kernel, in which case it would never appear in `lsmod` at all.
options.why: The guide's own trap: a built-in driver never appears in `lsmod` even though it is active, so absence from that list does not by itself mean a module is missing.

options.text: Assume the device needs a firmware update instead, since `lsmod` never lists device firmware either way regardless of what is loaded.
options.why: `lsmod` not listing firmware is expected and unrelated; the immediate next step is checking for a loadable module or a built-in driver before considering firmware.

options.text: Run `insmod` directly with a guessed module filename, since it behaves identically to `modprobe` in practice for any driver.
options.why: `insmod` loads exactly the file given with no dependency resolution, unlike `modprobe`, which resolves dependencies automatically — the two are not interchangeable.

options.text: Conclude the driver is definitely absent, since `lsmod` is supposed to be a complete list of every single driver active on the system right now, with no exceptions for how a driver was originally built into the kernel image.
options.why: This is precisely the mistake the guide warns against: a built-in driver is active but never appears in `lsmod`, so the list is not complete in that sense.

items.rationale: `lsmod` only lists loaded modules; a built-in driver never appears there even though it is active. `modprobe` loads a module and resolves dependencies automatically, unlike the more primitive `insmod`.

items.stem: Kconfig marks a hardware option `Y` at kernel build time rather than `M`. What does that mean for how its driver reaches the running system?

options.text: The driver is compiled directly into the kernel image and is active from boot, with no separate module to load or unload at runtime.
options.why: Kconfig's `Y` means built in; `M` would mean a loadable module instead — the two are alternatives, not a hierarchy where one is always preferred.

options.text: The driver still ships as a `.ko` file in this case, but `modprobe` loads it automatically on every single boot without ever being asked to.
options.why: A `.ko` file describes a loadable module, which is what `M` produces; a `Y` marking means no separate module file exists at all.

options.text: The driver is actually firmware now, embedded in the device itself rather than anywhere in the kernel image.
options.why: Firmware runs on the device's own controller and is a separate layer entirely; a Kconfig `Y` marking concerns kernel-side driver code, not device firmware.

options.text: `Y` is simply an older, deprecated way of marking a module that modern kernels now ignore entirely in favour of `M`.
options.why: Kconfig's tristate option genuinely supports either compiled-in (`Y`) or module (`M`) builds; `Y` is not deprecated, and either can be the correct choice depending on the driver.

items.rationale: A device driver can be built directly into the kernel image (`Y`) or as a loadable module (`M`) that attaches and detaches at runtime. A built-in driver is already part of the running kernel and has no separate module to list in `lsmod`.

items.stem: A new peripheral is detected by the kernel and its driver module loads successfully, but the device still does not function correctly. Loading the module again changes nothing. What layer might still be at fault?

options.text: The device's own firmware — low-level software embedded in the device itself, distinct from and running independently of the operating system.
options.why: Firmware runs on the device's own controller, below the OS entirely; no kernel module load can fix a problem that lives at that separate layer.

options.text: The kernel module itself, since simply reloading it again with slightly different options would eventually resolve any remaining fault it still has.
options.why: The scenario states the module already loaded successfully and reloading changes nothing; the driver having loaded correctly is what points elsewhere, toward firmware.

options.text: The shell used to run `modprobe`, since different shells are widely believed to load kernel modules differently.
options.why: Module loading is a kernel operation performed identically regardless of which shell invoked `modprobe`; the shell is not a plausible fault layer here.

options.text: Nothing further is possible to fix from the OS side or the device side; a successfully loaded driver means the OS's job here is fully done.
options.why: A loaded driver only means the kernel's side of talking to the device is working; the device's own firmware is a separate layer that can still be at fault.

items.rationale: Firmware is low-level software embedded in a device, distinct from the operating system above it. A driver operates the device from the OS side; if the device's own embedded software is missing or out of date, no module load fixes it — that is a separate firmware-update process.

items.stem: A team debates whether a new internal tool, running exclusively on headless cloud servers and administered over SSH, needs a GUI. What is the strongest justification for defaulting to CLI here?

options.text: No display server or desktop environment needs to run, saving memory and CPU the server has no other use for, and CLI output can be piped and scripted for automation.
options.why: The guide expects this reasoning specifically — scriptability, remotability, and resource cost — not merely the fact that servers 'don't have GUIs.'

options.text: The shell itself cannot run a GUI application under any circumstances, so CLI is therefore claimed to be the only option technically available on the machine in this situation at all.
options.why: GUI versus CLI names the interface paradigm as a whole; the shell is a specific CLI-side program and its existence does not by itself rule out a GUI running elsewhere on the machine.

options.text: A headless server has no terminal available, so CLI administration is not actually possible on it either, in that case.
options.why: A CLI session needs only a shell and a terminal, or an SSH connection carrying one — no display server required, which is exactly why CLI works on a headless machine.

options.text: Servers can never run a GUI at all, regardless of configuration, which settles the debate outright either way immediately.
options.why: A GUI can run on a server if a display server and desktop stack are installed; the real justification is cost and scriptability, not technical impossibility.

items.rationale: A CLI session needs only a shell and a terminal or SSH connection — no display server or desktop environment, which would otherwise consume memory and CPU the server has no other use for. CLI is also scriptable and remotable in ways a GUI is not.

items.stem: Are 'GUI vs CLI' and 'shell vs terminal' the same distinction asked two different ways?

options.text: No — GUI vs CLI names the interface paradigm as a whole, graphical or text-based; shell and terminal are both specifically components on the CLI side of that split.
options.why: The separating axis is level: one is a category the other sits inside of, not two names for one comparison.

options.text: Yes — a shell is simply treated as the CLI equivalent of a GUI, so comparing shell to terminal is really the same comparison stated again in different words entirely.
options.why: A shell interprets commands; a terminal displays them — both are CLI-side components, neither of which is 'the GUI equivalent' of the other.

options.text: No, but only because GUIs never involve a terminal of any kind whatsoever, under any circumstances.
options.why: A terminal is specifically a CLI-side component; its absence from GUI administration is consistent with the level distinction, but is not itself the reason the two comparisons differ.

options.text: Yes, since both comparisons ultimately ask whether the interface requires its own dedicated display server to run.
options.why: Shell vs terminal has nothing to do with a display server; that question only arises on the GUI side of the broader GUI-vs-CLI split.

items.rationale: GUI vs CLI names the interface paradigm as a whole. Shell and terminal are both specifically CLI-side components — one interprets, the other displays — so the two comparisons operate at different levels, not as restatements of each other.

items.stem: 'Which desktop environment does Ubuntu use' is asked as if it has one fixed answer. What makes that framing unreliable?

options.text: Most major distributions ship several desktop environments as installable options or spins, so the honest answer is 'whichever the specific install chose,' not a fixed mapping.
options.why: The guide names this directly as a distractor-heavy question style precisely because that fixed one-to-one mapping does not actually hold.

options.text: Desktop environment choice is fixed permanently at the kernel level and cannot vary between different installs of the same distribution's official installation image at all.
options.why: Desktop environment choice runs on top of a display server and is independent of the kernel entirely; nothing about it is fixed at that layer.

options.text: Ubuntu specifically has never offered more than one desktop environment option to install on any release.
options.why: Ubuntu ships official spins with different desktop environments (GNOME by default, others via spins), which is itself a counterexample to a single fixed answer.

options.text: The question is reliable; every distribution has exactly one desktop environment it ships with by design choice, always.
options.why: This restates the very assumption the guide flags as unreliable — most major distributions offer more than one installable desktop environment.

items.rationale: A desktop environment — window manager, panel, file manager, settings, and default applications — is a coherent product whose choice is independent of the distribution. Most major distributions ship several as installable options, so a fixed distribution-to-desktop mapping does not hold.

items.stem: A user wants to switch from GNOME to KDE Plasma on their existing installation without reinstalling the distribution. Is that generally supported?

options.text: Yes — swapping desktop environments on the same distribution and display server is generally supported, since the choice is independent of the distribution.
options.why: The guide states this directly: desktop environment choice is independent of which distribution is installed, and swapping is generally supported.

options.text: No — the display server itself would need reinstalling from scratch, since each desktop environment is assumed to require its own dedicated protocol underneath it.
options.why: A desktop environment runs on top of an existing display server, X11 or Wayland; it does not require reinstalling that underlying protocol layer.

options.text: No — swapping desktop environments requires switching to a different distribution family entirely first, before anything else.
options.why: Distribution family concerns package manager lineage; it has no bearing on which desktop environment is installed on top of a given distribution.

options.text: Yes, but only if the user also switches from CLI administration to GUI administration beforehand as a prerequisite.
options.why: GUI-vs-CLI administration and desktop environment choice are separate questions; nothing about swapping environments requires changing how the system is otherwise administered.

items.rationale: A desktop environment runs on top of a display server, providing the window manager and surrounding applications. Swapping desktop environments on the same distribution and display server is generally supported, since the choice is independent of the distribution.

items.stem: Between X11 and Wayland, which is the newer display server protocol intended to replace the older one?

options.text: Wayland — it is the newer replacement for the older X11 protocol.
options.why: This is the recognition-level fact the concept tests: know that Wayland is newer, not the protocol internals of either.

options.text: X11, since it was adopted more recently by most major distributions as their default.
options.why: Recent default adoption by a distribution does not change which protocol is older; X11 predates Wayland regardless of current default choices.

options.text: Neither is newer; both were released in the same year as competing standards.
options.why: They were not released in the same year; X11 is the long-established older protocol, and Wayland was developed later specifically to replace it.

options.text: The two names refer to the same underlying protocol under different branding.
options.why: X11 and Wayland are distinct display server protocols, not two names for one thing; the concept exists specifically to test that they are different and one is newer.

items.rationale: X11 and Wayland are the display server protocols underlying Linux graphics, with Wayland being the newer replacement for the older X11. This is recognition-level: know which is newer, not which distribution defaults to which.

items.stem: A variable is set with `MYVAR=value` in an interactive shell. `echo $MYVAR` shows the value, but a script the shell then runs cannot see it at all. Why, and which command would have fixed it?

options.text: It was never exported, so it is a shell variable rather than an environment variable and is not inherited by child processes; `export MYVAR` before running the script would fix it.
options.why: The guide's own trap: setting a variable without exporting it leaves it visible in the current shell via `echo` but invisible to any child process, including a script.

options.text: `env` was not run first, and running it would have exported every current shell variable automatically for the script.
options.why: `env` only prints, or runs a command with, the current environment; it does not export anything itself, and un-exported shell variables never appear in its output.

options.text: The script uses a different PATH, which prevented it from finding the variable's value anywhere in that path.
options.why: PATH governs how bare command names resolve to executables; it has no bearing on whether a variable is inherited by a child process.

options.text: Interactive shells and scripts are always supposed to share the exact same variables automatically, so an outcome like this one should genuinely never be possible in the first place.
options.why: Inheritance is one-directional and copy-based, and only exported variables are copied into a child process's environment at all — this is expected behaviour, not a fault.

items.rationale: A shell variable becomes an environment variable only once exported; from that point every child process the shell forks receives a copy. `echo $MYVAR` sees the un-exported variable in the same shell, but a script forked as a child process does not.

items.stem: Someone wants to see every environment variable currently exported in their session, without printing un-exported shell variables mixed in. Which command gives exactly that?

options.text: `env`, run with no arguments, which prints only exported environment variables.
options.why: `env` with no arguments prints the current environment specifically, excluding shell variables that were never exported.

options.text: `echo $HOME`, since it prints an environment variable and can simply be repeated for each one.
options.why: `echo $HOME` prints one specific variable's value; it does not enumerate the full set of exported variables the way `env` does.

options.text: `export`, run with no arguments, since it is the command that creates environment variables in the first place.
options.why: Bare `export` does list exported names on most shells, but it is the variant of the concept's own list-and-set command, not the dedicated 'print the environment' tool `env` is.

options.text: Any shell variable that has ever been referenced with `$` automatically shows up in `env` output.
options.why: Referencing a variable with `$` only reads its current-shell value; it does not export it, and un-exported variables are absent from `env`'s output regardless of how often they were referenced.

items.rationale: `env`, run with no arguments, prints the current environment — exported variables only, not un-exported shell variables. `echo` prints a single named value rather than enumerating the environment.

items.stem: A program was just installed to `/opt/tool/bin/tool`, but typing `tool` reports 'command not found' even though the file exists and is executable. What is the most likely cause, and what confirms it?

options.text: `/opt/tool/bin` is missing from PATH; `echo $PATH` would show the directory absent, and PATH is searched left to right for the first match on a bare command name.
options.why: This is the guide's central trap for the concept: 'command not found' for something genuinely installed usually means the installing directory is missing from PATH, not that the install failed.

options.text: The file must actually be corrupted, since `which tool` reporting nothing found always means the binary itself is broken somehow.
options.why: `which` reports nothing found when a directory is missing from PATH just as readily as when a file is broken; PATH is the far more common cause and should be checked first.

options.text: The shell needs to be restarted entirely, since PATH is believed to be fixed permanently at login time and never re-read afterward at all, under any circumstances whatsoever.
options.why: PATH can be updated within a running shell session by exporting a new value; a restart is not required to fix a PATH omission, only re-exporting or reloading the relevant config.

options.text: PATH is searched right to left, so a later directory's match should have been found first regardless of the order it was listed in.
options.why: PATH is searched left to right, with the first match winning; this scenario is about a directory being absent entirely, and the search order itself would not rescue a missing entry.

items.rationale: 'Command not found' for a genuinely installed program is almost always a PATH problem: the installing directory is missing from PATH. `echo $PATH` confirms it, and PATH is searched left to right for the first match.

items.stem: `which mycmd` reports nothing found, but typing `mycmd` at the prompt runs successfully. Which command would reveal what `mycmd` actually is, including cases `which` cannot see?

options.text: `type mycmd`, which reports how a name would be interpreted — builtin, alias, function, or file — seeing categories the external `which` cannot.
options.why: The guide names `type` specifically as seeing builtins and aliases that the external `which`, limited to searching PATH, cannot.

options.text: `which -a mycmd`, since adding `-a` extends `which` to also search shell builtins and aliases directly.
options.why: `-a` only lists every PATH match for an external command; it does not extend `which`'s visibility to builtins or aliases, which stay outside its scope entirely.

options.text: `echo $PATH`, since reading the full search list would reveal exactly where `mycmd` is hiding on disk.
options.why: If `mycmd` is a builtin or alias, it has no file on PATH at all to be found by reading the list; PATH inspection would not resolve this case.

options.text: Nothing else needs checking here — `which` finding nothing means `mycmd` does not actually exist as any kind of runnable command at all, in any form.
options.why: The command visibly ran, so it exists in some form; `which` finding nothing only means it is not an external file on PATH, which `type` can still identify.

items.rationale: `which` only searches PATH for external executables and has no visibility into shell builtins or aliases. `type` reports more generally what a name resolves to — builtin, alias, function, or file — which is why it succeeds where `which` reports nothing found.

items.stem: A teammate needs three separate facts about a server: its kernel release and hardware name in one line, its distribution identity, and how long it has been running. Which three commands supply those, respectively?

options.text: `uname -a` for kernel and hardware facts, `cat /etc/os-release` for distribution identity, and `uptime` for time since boot and load averages.
options.why: Each command is scoped to a distinct fact: `uname -a` for kernel/hardware, the distribution file for identity, and `uptime` for elapsed time and load.

options.text: `cat /etc/os-release` alone is assumed to answer all three, since it is believed to also report kernel version and uptime as part of that very same file.
options.why: That file reports distribution identity only; it does not include kernel version or uptime, which come from `uname` and `uptime` respectively.

options.text: `hostnamectl` alone answers all three, since it exists on every Linux system and reports everything at once for free, always.
options.why: `hostnamectl` is systemd-specific and absent on non-systemd distributions, and it does not report uptime or load averages, which `uptime` provides separately.

options.text: `uname -a` reports the distribution name directly, making a separate distribution check entirely unnecessary in every case.
options.why: `uname -a` reports kernel and hardware facts; it does not reliably report the distribution's name and release, which is what `/etc/os-release` is specifically for.

items.rationale: `uname -a` reports kernel name, hostname, kernel release, version, and machine hardware name together. `cat /etc/os-release` reports distribution identity specifically. `uptime` reports time since boot plus load averages — three commands for three distinct facts.

items.stem: `uptime` reports a load average of 4.0 on one server and 4.0 on another. Are both servers under equal relative load?

options.text: Not necessarily — load average is not normalised for CPU count, so 4.0 is a quarter of capacity on a 16-core machine and twice capacity on a 2-core one; `nproc`'s answer is needed to judge either figure.
options.why: The guide states this directly: `uptime`'s numbers mean nothing without also knowing the core count, since the same figure represents very different relative loads.

options.text: Yes — a load average of 4.0 is assumed to always mean the same relative load, since the figure is believed to be normalised by the kernel itself before it is ever reported back to a user at all, on any machine.
options.why: `uptime` does not normalise for core count; the raw figure is relative to the machine, which is exactly why two identical numbers can mean very different things.

options.text: Yes, since `hostnamectl` reports load averages in a normalised, comparable form across every different machine it runs on.
options.why: `hostnamectl` reports hostname, OS, kernel, and architecture; it does not report load averages at all, normalised or otherwise.

options.text: Not necessarily, but only because the two servers are certainly running different kernel versions of Linux entirely.
options.why: Kernel version has no bearing on how load average should be interpreted; the relevant missing fact is core count, not kernel release.

items.rationale: Load average is relative to the machine, not an absolute threshold — a load of 4 is a quarter of capacity on a 16-core machine and twice capacity on a 2-core one. `uptime`'s numbers mean nothing without also knowing `nproc`'s answer.
